plain: Ollama is a program that puts artificial intelligence inside your own computer. When you write to it, the answer doesn't travel to any company's servers: it gets computed right there, on your desk, with the computer you already have. It's the difference between ordering food delivery and having a kitchen at home: you pay nothing per dish, nobody sees what you're cooking, and it works even if the internet goes down, but you're limited to what fits in your kitchen. If your computer is modest, you'll have a modest cook, and it's best to accept that from minute one.

account.free: Completely free, no registration. No username, no password, no card, no daily message limit. You download the program, download the models, and that's it. The only thing you pay for is electricity and the disk space the models take up. There's a separate optional paid service, Ollama Cloud, for running huge models on someone else's servers when your machine isn't up to it: it ran around $20 a month, but the price has changed several times, so check ollama.com before trusting that figure. You don't need it for this course, and if you use it you lose exactly what makes Ollama special, which is that nothing leaves your computer.
steps: Go to ollama.com. The page is almost all white and has just one big black button in the center that says 'Download'. Don't confuse it with the 'Models' link at the top, which is just the catalog. Click 'Download'.

Three tabs appear: 'macOS', 'Windows', and 'Linux'. It usually picks yours automatically. Click the right one and a file between 200 and 700 MB (megabytes, about the size of a short movie) starts downloading. One or two minutes on fiber.

On Windows you download 'OllamaSetup.exe'. Double-click and a small window appears with an 'Install' button. It doesn't ask for administrator permissions or your computer's password: it installs inside your user folder. On Mac you download a .zip, open it, and drag the llama icon into the 'Applications' folder. The first time you open it, Mac will ask if you're sure you want to open an app downloaded from the internet: say yes.

Ollama doesn't open any big window once it finishes installing, and that throws people off. What you'll see is a small llama icon: on Windows, at the bottom right next to the clock, maybe hidden behind the '^' arrow that expands hidden icons; on Mac, at the top right in the menu bar. That icon means the engine is running in the background and waiting. If you don't see it, search for 'Ollama' in the start menu and open it.

Click the llama icon and a chat window opens, similar to any other. At the bottom, next to the box where you type, there's a dropdown with the model name. Choose a small one to start: 'llama3.2:3b' takes up about 2 GB and runs even on a laptop with 8 GB of memory. If you'd rather do it by typing commands, open the Terminal (on Windows search for 'Terminal' or 'PowerShell' in the start menu; on Mac it's in Applications, inside Utilities) and type: ollama run llama3.2:3b

The first time you'll see a progress bar with a percentage. It's about 2 GB, 2 to 10 minutes depending on your connection. This happens only once per model: after that it lives on your disk and starts in two seconds, with or without internet.

Type anything and press Enter. You'll see the words appearing one at a time, as if someone were typing on the other end. If you're in the Terminal, to exit the conversation type /bye, with the slash in front, and you're back at the normal command line. To see which models you have saved and how much space they take: ollama list. To delete one: ollama rm llama3.2:3b
account.warning: Every model you try stays on your hard drive forever until you delete it by hand. llama3.2:3b is 2 GB, llama3.1:8b about 4.7 GB, gemma3:27b about 17 GB. Three evenings of curiosity trying models and you've eaten up 30 or 40 GB without noticing, until your computer warns you it's out of space. Check what you have with 'ollama list' and delete what you don't use with 'ollama rm model-name'. That deletion is irreversible and doesn't go to the trash: if you regret it, you have to download the whole thing again. And a security warning: if a tutorial tells you to set OLLAMA_HOST to 0.0.0.0 to 'access it from your phone', don't do it while you're still learning. That opens your Ollama to the entire network you're on, and anyone connected to the same wifi (an office, a hotel, a café) can use your computer for whatever they want without you seeing it.

first: Open the chat window and type something short and silly, like 'explain what a mortgage is in three sentences'. Watch the speed at which the words come out: that's what your computer can deliver, and it's good to know that before getting your hopes up.
Cut the internet entirely: airplane mode, or turn off wifi. Ask it the same thing again. It answers the same way. That moment explains what Ollama is for better than any theory.

Check how much memory you really have before choosing anything else. On Windows, Ctrl+Shift+Esc opens Task Manager, 'Performance' tab, 'Memory' section. On Mac, Apple menu and 'About This Mac'. Write that number down: it controls everything else.
Type 'ollama list' in the Terminal and look at the size column. There you'll see exactly how many gigabytes your curiosity has cost. Get used to checking it every few days.

Give it a task it's good at and one it's not. Hand it a convoluted email and ask it to rewrite it in three lines: it'll do fine. Then ask it what the last month's interest rate was: it'll make it up. With those two examples you'll know what to trust it with.
shortcuts: ollama run model-name
The command that does it all: if the model isn't there, it downloads it; if it is, it loads it and opens the conversation. It's 80% of your daily use. Example: ollama run llama3.1:8b
/bye

Typed inside the conversation, with the slash in front, and it returns you to the normal Terminal line. The model stays in memory for about 5 minutes in case you come back. On Mac and Linux, Ctrl+D does the same.
Ctrl+C

Cuts off a response halfway without closing anything. You'll use it every day: as soon as you see the model has misunderstood the question, cut it off and rephrase instead of waiting through three useless paragraphs.
ollama list
The list of everything you have downloaded, with its size in gigabytes and when you downloaded it. It's your hard drive's receipt. Check it before downloading anything new.
ollama ps
Shows which model is loaded in memory right now and how much space it takes. When your computer starts acting weird, this command tells you in two seconds whether it's Ollama's fault.
ollama stop model-name
Unloads the model from memory instantly, without waiting the usual 5 minutes. It's the 'give me back my RAM' button when you're about to open Photoshop or a video call.
/set parameter num_ctx 8192

Inside the conversation, expands the model's field of view before you paste a long document. It defaults to short and cuts things off from behind without warning. It costs memory, so only raise it when you need it.
/set verbose

Inside the conversation, makes it show you, after every response, the real speed in word-chunks per second. It's the only honest way to compare two models on YOUR computer, instead of trusting internet tables.
/clear

Clears the current conversation's memory without exiting or reloading the model. Use it when switching topics: otherwise the model keeps dragging along the previous subject and it contaminates the answers.
Up arrow
In the Terminal, brings back the last command you typed. Saves you from retyping 'ollama run qwen2.5-coder:7b' forty times a day.
daily: One single model, one that fits comfortably, for 90% of the work. With 16 GB of memory that's llama3.1:8b or qwen2.5:7b. Switching models every couple of days is the best way to learn nothing: stick with one until you know exactly where it fails.

Rewriting, translating, shortening, and changing the tone of text YOU already have in front of you. It's what a small model does best, because it doesn't need to know anything about the world: just transform what you give it. Emails, product descriptions, review replies, legal text in plain language.

Repetitive, high-volume work: sorting 800 emails by topic, pulling the ID and amount from 300 invoices in text, tagging comments as positive or negative. This is where local wins decisively over the cloud, because the cost per item is zero and you can leave it running all night.

Expanding the context before pasting something long. Enter with 'ollama run your-model', type '/set parameter num_ctx 8192', and then paste the document. If you don't, the model only keeps the end of the text and answers as confidently as if it had read the whole thing.

Watching memory with 'ollama ps' and releasing it with 'ollama stop'. An 8B model keeps occupying almost 5 GB for 5 minutes after you finish. If your computer drags right when you close the conversation, this is why.

Disk cleanup once a month: 'ollama list', check what you haven't touched, and 'ollama rm name'. It's irreversible and doesn't go to the trash, but redownloading it takes ten minutes. Better that than running out of space on your system drive.

Split the work honestly: the confidential stuff, the repetitive stuff, and whatever has to work without internet, here; the hard stuff, the long stuff, and whatever can't afford to be wrong, on a paid cloud model. It's not a competition, they're two different tools.

templates.name: Decision table: which model based on your computer
templates.what: The answer to the only question that matters on day one. Good for anyone who doesn't know whether their machine can handle it and doesn't want to download 20 GB just to find out it can't. It's a napkin calculation: total memory minus 4 GB that Windows or macOS plus the browser keep for themselves, and what's left is your real ceiling.
templates.how: 1) Check your memory: Windows, Ctrl+Shift+Esc, 'Performance' tab, 'Memory'. Mac, Apple menu and 'About This Mac'. 2) Find your range below. 3) Copy the line starting with 'ollama pull' and paste it into the Terminal. 4) Once it's done, run it with 'ollama run' and the same name. Sizes are approximate and change with versions: check yours with 'ollama list' after downloading.
fill: The number shown in Task Manager or 'About This Mac'
Whether you have an NVIDIA graphics card and how many gigabytes
Task Manager, 'Performance', 'GPU'; look for 'Dedicated GPU memory'
General text, code, or reading images and scanned documents
templates.code:
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# FIRST: check your memory
#   Windows -> Ctrl+Shift+Esc -> Performance tab -> Memory
#   Mac     -> Apple menu -> About This Mac
# Rule: total memory - 4 GB (system and browser) = your real ceiling
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

# 8 GB RAM  (basic office laptop, usable ceiling ~4 GB)
ollama pull llama3.2:3b          # ~2 GB    general use, runs easily
ollama pull gemma3:4b            # ~3.3 GB  a bit better, tight fit
# With 8 GB don't try anything 7B or above. It won't fit.

# 16 GB RAM  (typical work laptop, usable ceiling ~12 GB)
ollama pull llama3.1:8b          # ~4.7 GB  the all-rounder
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b           # ~4.7 GB  very good in Spanish/other languages
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b     # ~4.7 GB  for code
ollama pull phi4                 # 14B, ~9 GB  better, but close Chrome

# 32 GB RAM (or 32 GB Mac, usable ceiling ~26 GB)
ollama pull gemma3:27b           # ~17 GB
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:32b    # ~20 GB  for code, very solid
ollama pull gpt-oss:20b          # ~14 GB

# 64 GB or more (or Mac Studio / expensive desktop rig)
ollama pull llama3.3:70b         # ~43 GB

# EXTRA: reading images and screenshots (needs ~2 GB more than its size)
ollama pull llama3.2-vision      # 11B, ~7.9 GB   needs 16 GB or more
ollama pull gemma3:4b            # ~3.3 GB        also reads images

# EXTRA: searching inside your own documents (indexing model)
ollama pull nomic-embed-text     # ~274 MB, fits on anything

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# DAILY MAINTENANCE
ollama list                      # what I have and how much it takes up
ollama ps                        # what's loaded in memory RIGHT NOW
ollama stop llama3.1:8b          # release the memory instantly
ollama rm gemma3:27b             # delete from disk (IRREVERSIBLE)
ollama show llama3.1:8b          # model card: context, license
# ---------------------------------------------------------------

templates.name: Modelfile: your company assistant, with the rules baked in
templates.what: A model of your own, with its own name, that already knows who you are, how you write, and what it shouldn't do, without you having to repeat it every conversation. Good for anyone who runs the same kind of task every day: customer service, product descriptions, review replies, internal notes.
templates.how: 1) Create a folder on the Desktop, for example 'my-assistant'. 2) Inside it, create a text file and name it Modelfile, with NO extension. Watch out with Windows Notepad: when saving, under 'Save as type' choose 'All Files' and type the name in quotes, "Modelfile", or you'll end up with a Modelfile.txt that doesn't work. 3) Paste the code below inside and change what's in brackets. 4) Open the Terminal, go to that folder with 'cd Desktop\my-assistant' and type: ollama create assistant -f Modelfile. Takes a few seconds and doesn't download anything new if you already have the base model. 5) Use it with: ollama run assistant. 6) If you regret it: ollama rm assistant. It only deletes your version, the base model stays.
fill: The base model that fits according to the table above. With 8 GB of RAM use llama3.2:3b
The name of your company or project
What you do and where. Example: dental clinic in Austin
The details you repeat a hundred times a day in emails
Raise it to 16384 if you're going to paste long documents and have 32 GB. Lower it to 4096 if you have 8 GB
The lower, the more literal and repetitive; the higher, the more creative and inventive. For serious work, between 0.2 and 0.5
templates.code:
FROM llama3.1:8b

PARAMETER num_ctx 8192
PARAMETER temperature 0.4
PARAMETER top_p 0.9

SYSTEM """
You are the internal assistant for [YOUR BUSINESS NAME], a [TYPE OF BUSINESS] in [CITY].

HOW YOU WRITE
- Always in professional English.
- Short sentences. No intros like "sure, here you go".
- No closing summaries or "hope this helps".
- Never use emojis.

WHAT YOU DON'T DO
- If you don't know something, write exactly: I DON'T KNOW. And stop there.
- Never make up prices, dates, deadlines, people's names, legal citations,
  or case numbers. Not even as an example.
- Never promise anything on the company's behalf: discounts, delivery
  times, or refunds unless I've given them to you in the message.

FIXED DATA YOU CAN USE
- Hours: [HOURS]
- Contact email: [EMAIL]
- Return policy: [SUMMARIZE IT IN ONE SENTENCE]

OUTPUT FORMAT
- When asked for customer-facing text, return it ready to copy and
  paste, with no comments around it and no explaining what you did.
- When asked for a list, return only the list.
"""

templates.name: Processing a whole folder of files, one by one, without touching anything
templates.what: A small script that grabs every .txt file in a folder, feeds it to your local model with the same instruction, and drops each result in another folder. This is the case where having AI at home clearly wins: 500 files through the cloud is dozens of dollars, here it's zero dollars and one night with the computer left on.
templates.how: 1) Copy the code into Notepad and save it on the Desktop as process.ps1 (under 'Save as type' choose 'All Files' and type the name in quotes). 2) Change the first five lines: the two folders, the model, and the instruction. 3) Right-click on the file, 'Run with PowerShell'. 4) If Windows tells you script execution is disabled, open PowerShell and type: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File "$HOME\Desktop\process.ps1". 5) You'll see one line per file with a counter. Let it run. This is Windows-only; if you're on Mac, ask the AI to translate it into a shell script and tell it the commands are the same.
